derivations.claim: If exact Lanczos runs through step $m$ without breakdown, [F1], [F2], and [F7] give an orthonormal basis $Q_m$ of $K_m$ and a symmetric compression $H_m=Q_m^{\mathsf T}AQ_m$. By [F3], each eigenpair of $H_m$ lifts to an exact Ritz pair of $A$; by [F4], the largest eigenvalue of $H_m$ is the maximum Rayleigh quotient on $K_m$, namely $\theta_m$. If Lanczos breaks down earlier, the definition of $\theta_m$ remains the maximum over the already formed Krylov space.

Assume $r<n$. By [F4], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $A$ whose first $r$ vectors span the range of $P$. If $Pb=0$, then $b$ is orthogonal to that eigenspace. For every integer $j\ge0$ and every top eigenvector $u$, symmetry gives $u^{\mathsf T}A^jb=(A^ju)^{\mathsf T}b=\lambda_1^j u^{\mathsf T}b=0$. Thus every vector in $K_m$ lies in the orthogonal complement of the top eigenspace, where all Rayleigh quotients are at most $\lambda_{r+1}$; this proves branch 1.
If $r=n$, every eigenvalue is $\lambda_1$, so [F4] gives $A=\lambda_1I$. Every nonzero $x\in K_m$ then has Rayleigh quotient $\lambda_1$, proving the stated dimension-one/full-multiplicity branch.

Assume $Pb\ne0$ and $\lambda_{r+1}>\lambda_n$. Apply [F5] with $a=\lambda_1$, $b=\lambda_{r+1}$, $c=\lambda_n$, and $k=m-1$ to obtain a polynomial $p_{m-1}$ of degree at most $m-1$ with $p_{m-1}(\lambda_1)=1$ and $|p_{m-1}(t)|\le\delta_m$ on $[\lambda_n,\lambda_{r+1}]$, where $\delta_m:=1/T_{m-1}(1+2(\lambda_1-\lambda_{r+1})/(\lambda_{r+1}-\lambda_n))$. By [F7], $x:=p_{m-1}(A)b$ belongs to $K_m$, and spectral decomposition gives $Px=Pb$ and $\|(I-P)x\|_2\le\delta_m\|(I-P)b\|_2$.

Assume $Pb\ne0$ and $\lambda_{r+1}=\lambda_n$. The spectral decomposition gives $A=\lambda_n I+(\lambda_1-\lambda_n)P$. Hence $Ab=\lambda_n b+(\lambda_1-\lambda_n)Pb$, so [F7] gives $Pb\in K_2$ and it has Rayleigh quotient $\lambda_1$; this proves $\theta_m=\lambda_1$ for $m\ge2$. For $m=1$, [F7] gives $K_1=\operatorname{span}\{b\}$, and the same decomposition gives the displayed exact formula for $\lambda_1-\theta_1$.

In the eigenbasis of [F4], write $x=Px+(I-P)x$. The two components are orthogonal, $A(Px)=\lambda_1Px$, and all eigenvalues on the second component lie in $[\lambda_n,\lambda_{r+1}]$. Therefore $$\lambda_1-\frac{x^{\mathsf T}Ax}{x^{\mathsf T}x} =\frac{\sum_{j>r}(\lambda_1-\lambda_j)x_j^2} {\|Px\|_2^2+\|(I-P)x\|_2^2} \le(\lambda_1-\lambda_n)\frac{\|(I-P)x\|_2^2}{\|Pb\|_2^2} \le(\lambda_1-\lambda_n)\delta_m^2\tau^2.$$ Since $\theta_m$ is the maximum Rayleigh quotient on $K_m$, it is at least the quotient of this nonzero $x$ and at most $\lambda_1$. This proves branch 2, including $m=1$ because $T_0=1$.

Finally, assume $r<n$, $Pb\ne0$, and exact Lanczos breaks down at column $d$. By [F2] and [F7], the vectors through $q_d$ form a basis of $K_d$ (for $d=1$, $K_1=\operatorname{span}\{b\}$); by [F6], $Aq_j\in K_d$ for $j<d$ and $Aq_d\in K_d$ because $w_d=0$. Hence $AK_d\subseteq K_d$, and [F7] plus induction gives $K_m=K_d$ for $m\ge d$. The spectral projector $P$ is a polynomial in $A$: if $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_s$ are the distinct eigenvalues of $A$, the Lagrange polynomial equal to $1$ at $\lambda_1$ and $0$ at every other $\mu_i$ acts as $P$ on the eigenbasis from [F4]. Therefore $Pb\in K_d$. Since $Pb\ne0$ and $A(Pb)=\lambda_1Pb$, the maximum Rayleigh quotient on $K_d$ is $\lambda_1$. This proves the exact-breakdown branch.

derivations.claim: The canonical convention [F1] identifies the stored count with $s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$. Each of at most $m$ columns uses one sparse matvec, which costs $O(s)$ by [F2] and [F3]. Summing over the columns gives $O(ms)$ work; if breakdown stops the run at $d<m$, the sum through $d$ is no larger.

At column $j$, one complete MGS pass computes $j$ length-$n$ inner products and $j$ length-$n$ vector updates, hence $O(jn)$ arithmetic; two passes multiply this by the fixed factor two. Therefore total orthogonalization work through $m$ columns is $O(n\sum_{j=1}^m j)=O(m^2n)$, and stopping earlier only reduces it.

In the no-breakdown branch, [F5] gives a projected matrix $\bar H_m\in\mathbb R^{(m+1)\times m}$ with nonzero subdiagonal entries $h_{j+1,j}$. For orthonormal $Q_{m+1}$ and $r_0=\beta q_1$, each candidate $x_0+Q_my$ has residual $$b-A(x_0+Q_my)=Q_{m+1}(\beta e_1-\bar H_my).$$ Therefore [F6] reduces GMRES minimization to this projected least-squares problem. The submatrix formed by rows $2,\ldots,m+1$ is upper triangular with diagonal $h_{2,1},\ldots,h_{m+1,m}$, so its columns are linearly independent. Thus $\bar H_m$ has full column rank. Applying one plane Givens rotation to each row pair eliminates one subdiagonal entry while preserving the Euclidean least-squares norm; the rotations create an upper-triangular $m\times m$ factor with nonzero diagonal. At column $j$, applying the previous at most $j-1$ rotations and forming the new rotation takes $O(j)$ scalar operations; all columns cost $O(m^2)$. Back substitution in the nonsingular triangular factor takes $O(m^2)$ operations, and forming the Krylov correction costs $O(mn)$. By [F6] this solves the specified GMRES projected least-squares problem.

Since $n\ge1$ and $m\le n$, $m^2\le m^2n$ and $mn\le m^2n$. Adding steps 1.1, 1.2, and 2.1 gives $O(ms+m^2n)$. Storing at most $m+1$ length-$n$ basis vectors takes $O(mn)$ slots; the Hessenberg and Givens data take $O(m^2)$ slots; temporary vectors use $O(n)$ slots. Since $m\le n$, both $m^2$ and $n$ are at most $mn$, proving the storage bound. If breakdown occurs at column $d<m$, the already formed basis and projected data use at most the same bounds with $d$ in place of $m$, and no fallback least-squares solve is included.

through step $m$ without breakdown, it is the largest Ritz value of
